\chapter{Dice Que --- Someone Else's Sentence, Inside Yours}
\label{ch:dice-que}
\hlchaptermodality{211}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report what someone says right now.}

I can report what someone says right now.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dice que]{dice que}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-dice-que}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Decir}, in the present, for one person. (\emph{Digo}, \emph{dices}, \emph{dice}.)

And one thing you can say about someone. (\emph{Está cansado}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one sentence inside another}]
You already have two whole sentences:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Dice.} — he says. \emph{Está cansado.} — he is tired.
\end{quote}

Reporting is nothing more than putting the second one \textbf{inside} the first, and the joint between them is \emph{que}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Dice que está cansado.}}
\end{quote}

Notice what did \textbf{not} happen. The inner sentence was not taken apart. \emph{Está cansado} went in whole, exactly as it would be said on its own.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
English lets the joint vanish. \emph{He says he's tired} is ordinary English, and so is \emph{He says that he's tired} — both are available.

\textbf{Spanish has only one of those.} \emph{Dice que está cansado} is the sentence; the version without \emph{que} is not a shorter way of saying it, it is not a sentence at all.

This is the second time you have met that refusal. When \emph{que} joined a noun to a clause — \emph{el libro que compré} — it could not be dropped either, while English happily says \emph{the book I bought}. Same word, same job description: \emph{que} is the piece that tells you a clause is arriving. Spanish will not begin a clause without announcing it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Dice que está cansado}
  \item the same thing about yourself
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sits at the joint between the two sentences? (\emph{\textbf{Que}}.)

And may it be left out, as English leaves out \emph{that}? (\textbf{No} — and you have now seen \emph{que} refuse to vanish twice.)
\end{tcolorbox}
